summary: Specifies a way to give FTP data ports addresses other than 32-bit IPv4 ones, using a long port command and a long passive reply. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This experimental RFC extends FTP's data-connection commands to describe more than IPv4 addresses and TCP ports. The new fields identify the address type and state the lengths of the address and port.

subtitle: Experimental FTP commands for data connections with variable-length addresses and ports.

tldr.problem: FTP's existing PORT command and PASV reply describe an IPv4 address and TCP port, which cannot represent every address family or variable-length address.
tldr.mechanism: LPRT and LPSV carry an address-family value and explicit lengths for the host address and port address. Reply code 521 reports unsupported address families.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1639 is Experimental and obsoletes RFC 1545. It proposes a general format for FTP over different network and transport protocols.

today: RFC 1639 is Experimental and obsoletes RFC 1545. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why FTP Needs Longer Addresses
sections.content:
FTP's PORT command specifies an address and data port for a transfer. Its address argument combines a 32-bit Internet host address with a 16-bit TCP port, represented as decimal fields separated by commas. The PASV reply uses the same format.

RFC 1639 proposes a way to describe address families other than the default Internet family, variable-length network addresses and variable-length port numbers. It also aims to allow FTP over transport interfaces other than TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The original FTP address fields were sized for an IPv4 address and TCP port. This proposal adds lengths so the commands can describe other formats.

sections.title: The LPRT Command Format
sections.content:
The LPRT command includes an 8-bit address-family value, an 8-bit host-address length, the host address, an 8-bit port-address length and the port address. Each field is represented as an unsigned decimal number, separated by commas; negative numbers are not allowed.

Address-family values from 0 through 15 are reserved for IP and assigned by IANA. Values from 16 through 255 are available for IANA assignment to other network-layer protocols. The lengths let the command represent host and port addresses whose sizes vary.
sections.plainLanguage: LPRT names the address family, gives the host address length and value, then gives the port length and value. The lengths tell the receiver where each part ends.

sections.title: LPSV and FTP Reply Codes
sections.content:
LPSV asks the server to listen on a data port and wait for a connection, like PASV, but its reply includes the long address fields. The suggested positive reply code is 228, with text indicating that long passive mode has begun.

Reply codes 500 and 501 cover syntax errors for LPRT and LPSV. Code 521 distinguishes a server that supports the commands but not the requested address family; its suggested reply lists the families the server supports.
sections.plainLanguage: LPSV lets the server announce a listening address in the longer format. If the server does not support the requested address family, it can return code 521 and list supported families.
